meta.title: Cold Email Hall of Fame Database
meta.description: Documented cold emails (plus a few famous cold calls and letters) that got replies from notable people. Every entry is paraphrased from a public source and linked. Full email bodies are not reproduced; follow the source link to read them.

verification_levels.primary: Told by the sender or recipient themselves, in their own published words or interview.
verification_levels.multi-source: Reported consistently by two or more independent outlets.
verification_levels.single-source: One secondary source; treat details as directional.
verification_levels.self-reported: Sender's own claim on their blog or newsletter, not independently confirmed.
verification_levels.gated: Featured by the source, but the email itself is behind a subscriber wall; only the public teaser is summarized.

tactic_glossary.credibility-first: The first line carries proof: a backer, a metric, a brand, a hard thing done.
tactic_glossary.specific-ask: One concrete, answerable request instead of 'pick your brain' or 'quick call'.
tactic_glossary.tiny-ask: The ask is deliberately small: 'can I send more?', one question, one tip.
tactic_glossary.subject-is-the-email: The whole request fits in the subject line so it can be answered from the inbox.
tactic_glossary.researched-personalization: References something real and specific about the recipient, found through research.
tactic_glossary.public-signal-match: The recipient had publicly said they want exactly this kind of email.
tactic_glossary.win-win-trade: Frames what the recipient gets, not just what the sender wants.
tactic_glossary.problem-first: Leads with a concrete, high-stakes problem before describing the product.
tactic_glossary.hard-metrics: Real numbers and named customers instead of vague traction claims.
tactic_glossary.short: Readable on a phone in under a minute.
tactic_glossary.persistence: Multiple polite follow-ups, each adding something new.
tactic_glossary.rejection-reply: Turns a 'no' into a new, lower-risk offer.
tactic_glossary.no-risk-offer: Removes the downside for the recipient (free trial work, no commitment).
tactic_glossary.proof-of-work: Ships something before asking: a demo, an essay, a video, a spec.
tactic_glossary.meet-then-email: Brief in-person contact followed by a sharp written follow-up.
tactic_glossary.humility: A brief, disarming acknowledgment of the cold approach.
tactic_glossary.curiosity-gap: Gives the reader a reason to want to know more.
tactic_glossary.transparent-self-interest: Says plainly why the sender wants this and how it fits their ambitions.
tactic_glossary.volume: Emails many plausible recipients; one reply is enough.
tactic_glossary.borrowed-credibility: Cites a known co-founder, institution or mutual connection.
tactic_glossary.topic-they-love: Opens on a subject the recipient genuinely enjoys talking about.
tactic_glossary.timing: Lands right when the recipient is primed (new fund, new company, public statement).

entries.sender_context: New Yorker staff writer who had never met Gates
entries.what_it_did: Skipped Microsoft PR and wrote straight to Gates's widely known address. Introduced himself as the writer working on the New Yorker piece about him and opened with a question about what makes email unique as a medium, a topic Gates loved.
entries.the_ask: Answer one open question about email
entries.outcome: A weeks-long email correspondence (three or four exchanges a week) that became the New Yorker article 'E-mail from Bill' (January 1994).

sources.title: E-mail from Bill (John Seabrook)
Cal Newport on the Seabrook profile

entries.sender_context: Special projects editor at Inc., unknown to Cuban
entries.subject_line: For Inc. mag: Can you pls. Share 3 Tips to Manage Your Inbox?
entries.what_it_did: Drafted ten versions with a colleague, then sent the entire request as the subject line. The body held only his signature so Cuban could see who was asking.
entries.response: Reply in 7 minutes (sent 4:03 pm, answered 4:10 pm)
entries.outcome: Cuban's tips ran in Inc. Hagerman distilled the lesson to: be clear, be brief, be direct.

sources.title: Inc: How I Got Mark Cuban to Answer My Email in 7 Minutes Flat

entries.sender_context: 25-year-old first-time founder of Factmata, no US network
entries.what_it_did: Opened by apologizing for the cold message, then stacked credibility fast: Google-backed, three NLP researchers with 30+ published papers. Tied the pitch to Cuban's own recent public comments on fake news. Under 150 words.
entries.the_ask: Permission to share more about the company
entries.outcome: $250K immediately and another $250K nine months later. Ghulati raised his whole ~$1M seed through cold email; he also emailed Craig Newmark and Biz Stone.

sources.title: AngelBacked: The Cold Emails That Actually Got Founders Funded

entries.sender_context: CEO of Mapistry (environmental-compliance SaaS)
entries.what_it_did: Her first email two years earlier was vague and went nowhere. The rewrite used a plain descriptive subject, led with the problem (compliance run on spreadsheets, multi-million-dollar lawsuit risk), then named Fortune 500 customers, a $3.7B market and specific growth numbers.
entries.the_ask: A 30-minute call, with two specific times offered
entries.response: Lemkin replied and later published it as one of the two best cold emails he had received
entries.outcome: Lemkin funded the company; Mapistry raised a $2.5M seed. The same template, tweaked per investor, hit a reported 33% success rate.

entries.sender_context: Founder of the 20VC podcast and fund
entries.what_it_did: Sent 53 emails, roughly weekly for a year. Each one varied the personal hook (a whiskey they both liked, a favorite holiday spot, recent results) and he A/B tested which personalization landed. Clear ask, short copy, credibility via audience numbers and past guests.
entries.outcome: Benioff appeared on 20VC in 2023 and publicly credited Stebbings's persistence.

entries.what_it_did: Emailed the CEO repeatedly but never rudely or too often. Upgraded his signature to a legitimate title (event producer with a startup association) and finally said he'd be 'in the neighborhood' and could stop by.

entries.outcome: Komisar later emailed the student unprompted with a relevant article. Ferriss's point: getting those replies rewires your sense of what's possible.

recipient_facts.fact: Keeps a public email address; as of 2020 got up to ~1,000 pitches a day, deletes ~90% and decides in a couple of seconds.
Publicly says he reads cold emails and has funded companies from them; prefers ~150-200 words with at least two concrete metrics.
Lists on his own website what he wants help with, a model for researching what a recipient values.
Auren Hoffman: most read every well-formed email; the recipient should benefit more than the sender, or wait until you have something that benefits them.
